title: The Shell
text: The shell (also called the command line or terminal) lets you talk to your computer by typing commands instead of clicking. We use it to run Git, launch R and Quarto, and move around the file system.

title: The Shell
text:
Opening a shell

macOSWindows


Use Terminal, which comes preinstalled on every Mac.

Press ⌘ + Space to open Spotlight.
Type Terminal and press Return.



Windows has several shells, but for this course use Git Bash, which behaves like the macOS/Linux shell.

Install Git for Windows (this also gives you Git Bash).
Open the Start menu, type Git Bash, and press Enter.

title: The Shell
text:
A few starter commands



Command
What it does




pwd
Print the current (working) directory


ls
List files in the current directory


cd folder
Change into folder


cd ..
Move up one directory


cat
Prints the contents of a file

title: The Shell
text:
Tips

Press Tab to autocomplete file and folder names.
Press the Up arrow to recall previous commands.
Paths are case-sensitive on the shell — Data and data are different.

title: The R App
text: When you install R, you also get a small graphical application bundled with it: R.app on macOS and Rgui on Windows. It gives you an R console plus a simple editor for writing scripts, without installing anything else. It is the quickest way to start writing R on your own machine.

title: The R App
text:
Opening the R App

macOSWindows



Open Finder and go to the Applications folder.
Double-click R (the blue R icon). This is R.app.
You can also press ⌘ + Space to open Spotlight, type R, and press Enter.

If you have both R.app and R64.app, either one is fine on a modern Mac.



Click the Start menu and type R.
Choose R x.y.z (the version number will match what you installed). This opens Rgui.
You can also find it under All Apps → R → R x.y.z.

If Windows shows both R i386 and R x64, choose R x64.



When the app opens you will see the R console with the > prompt. Type an expression and press Enter to run it:
2 + 2

title: The R App
text:
Writing an R script
The console is good for one-off commands, but anything you want to keep should go in a script — a plain text file with the .R extension that holds a sequence of R commands.
To open a new, empty script:

macOS: File → New Document, or press ⌘ + N.
Windows: File → New script, or press Ctrl + N.

An editor window opens. Type your code there, one command per line:
x <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42)
mean(x)
Nothing runs as you type. To run a line, put your cursor on it and press:

macOS: ⌘ + Enter
Windows: Ctrl + R

To run several lines, select them first and use the same shortcut. The commands are sent to the console, where you will see the output.

title: The R App
text:
Saving your script
Save early and often.

macOS: File → Save, or ⌘ + S.
Windows: File → Save, or Ctrl + S.

In the save dialog:

Choose a folder you can find again — a stat133 folder in your Documents is a good habit.
Give the file a short, descriptive name with no spaces, ending in .R, such as vector-practice.R.
Click Save.

To reopen it later, use File → Open Document (macOS) or File → Open script (Windows) and select the file.

title: The R App
text:
Tips

Use # to start a comment. Everything after it on that line is ignored by R.
Keep the script as the record of what you did; treat the console as scratch paper.

title: Positron
text: Positron is the code editor (IDE) we use to write and run R and Quarto. It is built by Posit, the same company behind RStudio, and is designed for data science.

title: Positron
text:
Installing Positron

Go to https://positron.posit.co.
Download the installer for your operating system.
Run the installer and open Positron.

Make sure you already have R installed so Positron can find it. If your computer is too old to run Positron, don’t fret. You can log into DataHub and work with Positron there.

title: Positron
text:
The layout

Editor: where you write scripts and .qmd documents.
Console: a live R session for running code interactively.
Variables / Environment: shows the objects currently in memory.
Plots, Help, and a Terminal are available in the side panes.

title: Positron
section: Opening a folder from a GitHub repository
text:
Opening a folder from a GitHub repository
Most of the projects in this course start by copying (“cloning”) a repository from GitHub onto your computer and opening it as a Positron folder.

On GitHub, open the repository and click the green Code button. Copy the HTTPS URL, which ends in .git.
In Positron, click the button in the upper left corner for New > New Folder from Git, then paste the URL in the top box.
Choose a folder on your computer to put the repository in — somewhere you’ll find again, like Documents/stat133/. Positron creates a new subfolder named after the repository.
Click OK.

The first time you clone, Git may ask for your GitHub username and a personal access token; see Git and GitHub for how to set that up.

Knowing which folder you’re in
Positron always has exactly one folder open, and everything — the console’s working directory, the file paths in your code, which repository git commands act on — is relative to that folder.
Check which one it is in the top-right corner of the window, next to the interpreter selector: it shows the name of the open folder alongside the running R session. You can also confirm from the console:
getwd()
If that isn’t the folder you expect, use File → Open Folder to switch. Opening a file from another project does not change the open folder.

title: Positron
text:
Running code

Put your cursor on a line and press ⌘ + Return (macOS) or Ctrl + Enter (Windows) to run it in the console.
Open a .qmd file and click Render to preview a Quarto document.

title: Positron
text:
Tips

Use the built-in Terminal pane to run shell and Git commands without leaving the editor.

title: Git and GitHub
text:
Git is a version-control system that tracks changes to your files, and GitHub is a website for hosting Git repositories. Together they let you save snapshots of your work and share it.
The best way to be sure you’re set with Git and GitHub is to fill out and follow the form here.

title: Git and GitHub
text:
Installing Git
On DataHub, Git is already installed. To install it on your own machine:

macOSWindows


Open Terminal and run:
git --version
If Git is missing, macOS will offer to install the developer tools. Accept and let it finish, then run the command again to confirm.


Install Git for Windows, which also provides Git Bash. Open Git Bash and confirm with:
git --version

title: Git and GitHub
text:
One-time setup
Tell Git who you are:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@berkeley.edu"

title: Git and GitHub
text:
The core workflow



Step
Command
Meaning




Clone
git clone <url>
Copy a repository to your machine


Stage
git add <file>
Mark changes to be saved


Commit
git commit -m "message"
Save a snapshot with a note


Push
git push
Upload commits to GitHub


Pull
git pull
Download others’ commits



Check the state of your repository at any time with:
git status

title: Git and GitHub
text:
Github
Go to https://github.com/ to set up a free account. Whichever email address you use to create your account, it should agree with same as the email you used in git config --global user.email "you@berkeley.edu". If you expect to not use Github after leaving Berkeley, then just use your Berkeley email. If you think you might use it after graduation, use your personal email.

title: Git and GitHub
section: Authenticating with a personal access token
text:
Authenticating with a personal access token
GitHub will not accept your account password from the command line. Instead you use a personal access token (PAT): a long string of characters that acts as a password for Git. You create it in the browser, then paste it into the terminal whenever Git asks for a password.

1. Create the token in your browser

Sign in at https://github.com/ and go to https://github.com/settings/tokens?type=beta (Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens).
Click Generate new token.
Fill in the form:

Token name: something you’ll recognize, like stat133-positron.
Expiration: pick a date after the end of the semester.
Repository access: All repositories.
Permissions: under Repository permissions, set Contents to Read and write. Leave everything else alone.

Click Generate token, then copy the token that appears.







Warning



The token is shown only once. Copy it now. If you lose it, delete it on GitHub and generate a new one — that’s normal and costs you nothing.




2. Paste it at the prompt
Do something that talks to GitHub, such as cloning one of your repositories or running git push from inside one. In Positron’s Terminal pane:
git clone https://github.com/USERNAME/REPO.git
Git will prompt you twice:
Username for 'https://github.com': your-github-username
Password for 'https://github.com': <paste your token here>
Paste the token, not your GitHub password. Nothing will appear on screen as you paste — that’s expected. Press Return.
That’s it. Git will ask you to paste the token again for each push or clone until the token expires — for a handful of assignments that’s a minor annoyance, not a problem.






TipDon’t want to paste it every time?



You can ask Git to remember the token so you’re only prompted once:

macOS: git config --global credential.helper osxkeychain
Windows: git config --global credential.helper manager

Run the command once, then paste the token at the next prompt. Git stores it and won’t ask again.

title: Git and GitHub
text:
Tips

Commit early and often, with short but descriptive messages.
git status is your friend — run it whenever you’re unsure what’s going on.
Treat your PAT like a password: don’t paste it into a script, a .qmd file, or a repository.

title: Syllabus
text:
An introduction to computationally intensive applied statistics. Topics will include organization storage of data, visualization and graphics, statistical learning and data mining, model validation procedures, and the presentation of results. This course uses R as its primary computing language.


Class Format
This is an in-person class with three lectures each week and one two-hour lab led by a GSI. This class is designed assuming you’ll be in class. If you miss class, you’ll be able to find most materials from class - slides, snippets of code - published on the course wesite.

Homework Parties
Tutors will offer Homework Party sessions several times each week. This is an opportunity to finish up any assignments that you’ve started in class or review any topics that are confusing for you. You’re welcome to attend any session that works well for your schedule. Check the Office Hours page to see the homework party schedule.
Homework Parties are a great place to go to meet other students and collaborate on assignments with tutors on hand to help you get unstuck.


Office Hours
Office hours are an opportunity to chat one-on-one with your instructor and GSIs. Please come to office hours! Coming to office hours does not send a signal that you are behind or need extra help. On the contrary, coming to office hours early and often tends to co-occur with success in the course. We’re happy to chat about the course material, statistics in general, careers in statistics, and whatever other statistics or data science topics are on your mind! Please check the Office Hours page to see the times of the various office hour/homework party sessions.



Materials

Computational tools
Each student will need a laptop in order to engage with the computing aspects of this class. Throughout the semester you’ll be installing several different software tools, all of which are free. We will be mainly using the computing and programming environment R (via RStudio) to analyze data in this class. We will also ask you to use a command line interface to interact with your operating system. You do need your own computer to use R and do the assignments. No need to install these ahead of time; we’ll guide you through how to get set up.
About half of the students in 133 have some coding experience in Python or R and about half do not. For those who come from Data 8 or some previous coding experience in python, the first labs will help you transfer that knowledge over to R. Both languages are excellent platforms for analyzing data, are widely used in data science, and have their individual strengths. R has been developed within the statistics community specifically for data analysis, while python is a general-purpose programming language but has large data analysis capabilities.


Supplementary texts
Your primary reference throughout the course will be the notes that you take in class but there are also several terrific books that are free and online that can expand your knowledge.

Advanced R, Hadley Wickham
R for Data Science, Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund
R packages, Hadley Wickham and Jenny Bryan
R Coding Basics, Gaston Sanchez




Course communication

bCourses
We don’t use bCourses for much. It is primarily used to disseminate important announcements for the entire class such as the initial welcome announcement, final exam information etc.


Discussion forum
The official discussion forum for the class will be hosted on Ed. Ed is a forum to ask and answer questions with your fellow students and course staff. It’s a useful resource for learning from your peers and seeking help from tutors and instructors.
If you have a question about the material or assignments (or anything related to the course), create a new post to ask your question on Ed. If it is about something personal, then mark it as “private”, and only course staff will be able to see your post. This is the best way to contact us if you have a personal concern, as it ensures the fastest response. If your question does not include personal information and can be answered by other students, make sure it is public.
In a course this large, the instructors have a difficult time responding to individual emails, so please use the class forum or visit office hours if you wish to contact us.



Assignments, Exams, and Grading

Turning-in assignments
You will be turning in your assignments on a platform called Pensive, the younger sibling of Gradescope. Note that regrade requests will need to be submitted by a deadline, which will usually be about a week the grades are released.


Problem Sets
Problem sets provide you with essential practice on the ideas and techniques discussed in class. They will be due roughly every week or two
You’re encouraged to work on your Problem Sets during one of the Group Tutoring sessions


Projects
Projects are open-ended assignments assignments designed to apply the concepts from the lecture notes in the cause of doing an analysis of real data. This will involve both writing code and communicating your thoughts and findings in English. Your Projects will be due before your corresponding Project Studio, roughly every 2-3 weeks.
You’re encouraged to work on your Projects during one of the Homework Party sessions.


Quizzes
Quizzes reinforce the most important concepts from the lecture. They cover the material from lecture, problem sets, and projects up until the time of the quiz.
Quizzes in this course will be administered in the Computer-Based Testing Facility (CBTF). Students are responsible for reading and following all CBTF policies and procedures, including instantiating a PrairieTest account, submitting any DSP accommodations in advance, and reserving and attending exam sessions on time. During CBTF quizzes, students may use only the materials and resources expressly authorized by the course; unauthorized devices, materials, or resources are prohibited. CBTF proctors monitor all sessions and will document and report any suspected academic misconduct to the course staff. Suspected violations will be handled in accordance with the Berkeley Honor Code and the UC Berkeley Code of Student Conduct, and may result in penalties up to and including a failing grade on the quiz or in the course and referral to the Center for Student Conduct.


Final Exam
The paper-and-pencil final exam will be held in person during finals week. It is a comprehensive exam and covers the material from the lecture, problem sets, and projects.
The final exam is scheduled for Monday December 14th from 7-10 pm.


Grading
Your final grade in this class is, to the best of our ability, a measure of your understanding of the concepts of computing with data. As such, the lions share of your grade comes from measures of your individual understanding: quizzes and the final. The project studios are also very important. They give us a sense of how well you understand the work you’ve done and give you practice talking through your reasoning in front of an audience.
The best way to prepare for these assessments is to earnestly engage with the problem sets and projects. Their role in the course is practice and they’ll be your single most effective way to learn. We want to see that you are keeping to a sensible schedule, so the problem sets will be submitted and graded credit/no credit, where full credit is given for any submission. The projects will not be graded per se, but they will need to be completed in order to discuss them at your Project Studio.

Problem Sets: 1%
Project Studio: 20%
Quizzes: 49%
Final: 30%

The grades will not be curved (> 90% is some kind of A, 80-90 is some kind of B, etc.), so there is no limit to the number of As and Bs that are earned.



Policies

Late Work
Rigorously completing the problem sets and projects is for your own benefit. Since they must be completed in order to take the Quizzes and participate in Project Studio, no late work is accepted.


Collaboration policy
On problem sets and projects, we strongly encourage collaboration between students. One of the best ways to learn is to talk things through with someone else. At the same time, these are your best opportunity to practice and learn, so be cautious not to lean to heavily on the understanding of a peer when working through your assignments.


AI policy
Please be thoughtful when using AI tools for your schoolwork. Doing so on problem sets and projects robs you of a valuable opportunity to learn and undermines your performance on exams. At the same time, they can be helpful in providing feedback on your writing.
At the end of the course, we’ll bring in AI tools for coding and learn how to use them. They’re very powerful, but you need firm mental models of the way code works before you’re able to use them well. For that reason, we suggest you refrain from using them until they’re introduced in class.


Accomodations for students with disabilities
Stat 133 is a course that is designed to allow all students to succeed. If you have letters of accommodation from the Disabled Students’ Program, please share them with your instructor as soon as possible, and we will work out the necessary arrangements.


Staying healthy
Maintaining your health and that of the Berkeley community is of primary importance, so if you are feeling ill or have been exposed to illness, please do not come to class. You’re encouraged to reach out to fellow students to discuss the class materials or stop by the homework parties or office hours to chat with a tutor or the instructor.



Frequently Asked Questions

What should I do if I’m on the waitlist?
Attend both lecture and lab and submit all assignments on time. Unfortunately we cannot grow the size of the class any more, so places will become available only when students drop. If you have an urgent need for the course, visit the drop in advising sessions in our department: https://statistics.berkeley.edu/academics/undergrad/advising.
What should I do if I’m a Concurrent Enrollment student?
Please do the same as the waitlisted students. If / when the waitlist clears, contact the instructor to be added to the class.
Are class sessions recorded?
No.
Is attendance in lecture required?
No.
Are time conflicts allowed?
No.
What if I join the class late?
If you join the class within the first two weeks, read through all of the material on the course website that you’ve missed. Also ask a neighbor in lecture if you can borrow their notes. Finally, visit the Homework Parties to discuss any topics you’ve missed. If you’ve missed any assignments in the first two weeks, request an extension from your GSI.
After two weeks into the semester, you’ll have too much material that you’ll need to make up, so you will have to wait to a subsequent semester to take the course.



Campus Resources
UC Berkeley has a vast wealth of resources to help with all aspects of student life. You can read about them at the links below.

Center for Educational Justice & Community Engagement

title: Project: Gerrymandering
text:
Very soon Californians will go to the polls to vote for their representative to the United States Congress. This election will determine whether the Republicans retain control of the House of Representatives. This is the first election held using district maps that are explicitly partisan. One year ago, Californians passed Proposition 50, which adopted a congressional district map drawn by the state legislature (bill AB 604). The purpose of this bill was to increase the partisan advantage of Democrats as a counterweight to a similar district map that was passed by the state of Texas to advantage the Republicans.
Your general research question for this project is:
Will the adoption of the new district map lead to an increase in partisan advantage relative to 2024? If so, by how much?
As always, you will be invited by email to a template repo corresponding to this project. This time, project.qmd is set to format: dashboard, the format from the Dashboards lecture. Each part below is a page of your dashboard. How you lay out each page is up to you, but each should show your results as explanatory displays (plots, tables, value boxes, or a few sentences) along with the code that produced them. The comment at the top of the template’s project.qmd has some tips on how to set this up.
Your dashboard opens on its Results page (Part 6), because that is where a reader starts, but you’ll build that page last: work through the parts in order.
In the assignment below, “On this page” describes what each page of your dashboard should show. The questions are there to prompt you to fully explore each phase of the analysis to be ready to answer questions about it during the Project Studio.

Context

California Statewide Special Election (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/prior-elections/statewide-election-results/statewide-special-nov-4-2025): official website for the election from the CA Secretary of State.
Statewide Database Precinct Data (https://statewidedatabase.org/d20/g24.html): source of precinct-level data from the 2024 General Election.
2024 Election Geographic Data (https://statewidedatabase.org/d20/g24_geo_conv.html): source of shapefiles for precinct maps from 2024 General Election.
Proposed Congressional Map (https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/proposed-congressional-map): source of shapefiles for district map proposed in AB 604.



Data
The template’s data/ folder holds:

state_g24_sov_data_by_g24_srprec.csv: Voting results (Statement of Vote) for the 2024 general election by registration precinct (SR precinct), from the Statewide Database (source: https://statewidedatabase.org/d20/g24.html). Its columns are described in the Statewide Database’s codebooks (https://statewidedatabase.org/info/codebooks.html).
g24-results-by-district.xlsx: Voting results at the district level, broken down by county.
g24-candidates-by-district.csv: Names of candidates running in each district race.

In Parts 5 and 6 you’ll download more files and add them to data/ yourself, unzipping any shapefiles into a subdirectory called data/shapefiles. Many of these files are too large for GitHub, so the template’s .gitignore keeps git from committing anything in data/ beyond the three files above. Keep every download inside data/: a file saved anywhere else would be committed. If you save a cleaned version of a data set, which is good practice, write it to data/clean/; that folder is committed.


Part 1: About the Data
Visit the website of the California Secretary of State for their information on last year’s special election and Proposition 50 and learn about the process, the documents that they make available, and the data that they make available.
Next visit the website of the Statewide Database and learn about what data products are available from the 2024 General Election and any extra information they provide about how to interpret them. Also learn about who runs the database, where it is housed, and how it operates.
On this page: provide an introduction to the election and the data for a reader who is new to both: what Proposition 50 changed and why, who publishes the data you use and how it comes to be, the units of geography it is recorded in and how they relate to one another, and a table of the data files you use, each with its source and what one row represents. Add to the table as you go, including the files you download in Parts 5 and 6. This page needs no code.
Some questions to consider:

What did Proposition 50 do, and how long does the AB 604 map stay in effect?
Who drew the AB 604 map, and how is that different from how California’s congressional maps were drawn before?
What documents and data does the Secretary of State publish about the election?
Who runs the Statewide Database, where is it housed, and what is it for?
What data products does it publish for the 2024 General Election?
What do its notes say about the limits of the data?
How do census blocks, SV precincts, SR precincts, congressional districts, and counties relate to one another? Which nest inside which?
Why is an SR precinct always a geographic area, while an SV precinct may not be?
Votes are counted and reported by SV precinct. How does the Statewide Database produce the SR precinct counts you’ll use, and what does that mean for how you should read them?



Part 2: Data Cleaning
Read in the vote count data from the 2024 General Election at the SR precinct level (state_g24_sov_data_by_g24_srprec.csv). You’ll use this same data set for the rest of the project, including re-running the election on the new map in Part 5. Clean the data frame using the audit checklist from the data cleaning lecture to ensure values are recorded correctly for the rest of the analysis.
On this page: the decisions you made in cleaning the data. For each problem you found, show the evidence for it (a table, a plot, or a count), what you did about it, and how many rows it affected, along with the code for each step. Close with the size of your clean data set.
Tips

Read the website of the statewide database carefully for disclaimers about the state of the data.
Inspect columns to ensure they’re the correct type. If they’re not, investigate why not and correct it.
Inspect the values in each column to ensure they have the values that you would expect.
Check that columns that you expect to have unique values indeed don’t have replicates.



Part 3: Exploratory Data Analysis
Now that you have a clean data set for precinct-level vote totals from the 2024 election, now is your opportunity to scratch your curious itch and ask a few questions that can be answered with summary statistics or visualizations.
On this page: a check of your clean data against the official district totals, followed by at least three questions of your own. For each question, show the question, an explanatory display that answers it, and your answer in a sentence or two.
Some examples to get you thinking:

When you add up your precincts by district, do your totals agree with those in g24-results-by-district.xlsx? Where they don’t, why not?
How many precincts/counties/districts featured two candidates from the same party?
Which precinct/county/district had the closest race?
What is the range of total sizes of the precincts?
Which races were the closest?
Which races were the biggest blowouts?
What proportion of incumbents were re-elected?
Be creative here!



Part 4: Measuring Partisan Advantage
For the 2024 general election, calculate the mean-median score and efficiency gap associated with the 2024 map of congressional districts. You should have everything you need in your cleaned precinct-level data frame.
On this page: the partisan advantage under the 2024 map: the seats and the share of the two-party vote that each party won, the mean-median score, and the efficiency gap. Show each statistic alongside a display that shows where it comes from, such as the distribution of vote shares across districts or the votes each party wasted.
Tip: it may be helpful to write a function that takes a vector of votes across districts for party A and a vector of votes for party B, and returns a vector of the number of votes wasted by party A in each district.


Part 5: Re-running the 2024 Election
Calculate what the election results would have been had the 2024 election been run using the district map proposed in AB 604. There are two approaches that can be taken. Both start from the SR precinct data you cleaned in Part 2: SR precincts are always geographical, so their votes can be placed on a map.
The data files listed below are not in the template repo; you’ll be downloading them directly. Put csv files in data/ and unzip any shapefiles into data/shapefiles/, not anywhere else in your repo: inside data/, git ignores them, and some are far too large for GitHub (the SR precinct shapefile is over 300 MB). The AB 604 zip unpacks into an AB604/ folder, so its shapefile is data/shapefiles/AB604/AB604.shp, alongside a __MACOSX/ folder you can delete. Its districts are in a Web Mercator projection, so transform them with st_transform(crs = 3310) before combining them with other layers. Some of this code is slow to run, so the template marks this part’s code cell with cache: true: it reruns only when you change it or the Part 2 cleaning it builds on.
Of these two approaches, Approach A is slightly more direct but induces a bit more error than Approach B. You can choose one to pursue. If you end up doing both, I’d be very interested in an analysis that compares the results. Please email me directly if you do this to share your work.
Approach A: Area-weighted Interpolation
Premise: if we assume the voters are spread evenly across their precincts, we can allocate a precinct’s votes to a congressional district in proportion to the percentage of the area of that precinct that is in the district. Along with your clean SR precinct data, you will need two files:

SR Precinct Shapefiles: Shapefiles for the SR precincts (source: https://statewidedatabase.org/d20/g24_geo_conv.html).
Proposed Congressional Map: source of shapefiles for district map proposed in AB 604 (source: https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/proposed-congressional-map).

General approach:

Join the geometries from the shapefile to your clean SR precinct data.
Load geometries of the proposed congressional map.
Ensure both geometries are valid and use the same projection (I recommend st_transform(crs = 3310)).
Use area-weighted interpolation to populate the vote counts of each district in the proposed map.

Note: the people at the Statewide Database are working to correct some errors in the geometries of the SR precincts. sf can do a quick job of it using the following:

sr_shp <- sr_shp |>
  st_transform(3310) |>          # switch to equal area projection first
  st_set_precision(1) |>         # snap points to 1 m grid
  st_make_valid() |>             # fix self-intersections/bow-ties
  st_collection_extract("POLYGON")

Approach B: Proportional Allocation
Premise: we can improve on the uniform distribution assumption by working with a smaller geographic unit, census blocks. While we don’t know the number of votes for each candidate at the census block level, we do know the proportion of registered voters at each census block. We can allocate the votes from the SR precincts across the blocks relative to the proportion of registered voters that live on that block.
Along with your clean SR precinct data, you will need two files:

SR Precinct to Block Correspondence: Number of registered voters by (partial) block (source: https://statewidedatabase.org/d20/g24_geo_conv.html).
Block membership in AB 604 districts: A list of the census block keys and their new congressional district as of AB 604 (source: https://aelc.assembly.ca.gov/proposed-congressional-map).

General approach:

Working from the census block data, add SR voting data to each (fractional) block in proportion to the percentage of registered voters in the precinct that live on that block.
Identify which new district each block is in.
Tally up the votes for each new district.

Note: there are some census blocks that are split between multiple SR precincts. Accordingly, each row of the SR Precinct - Block correspondence file is actually a potential fractional block: most rows represent an entire block, but some represent the portion of a block that is in a particular precinct. BLKTOTREG is the total number of registered voters in the full block; SRTOTREG is the total number of registered voters in the SR precinct. PCTSRPREC is the percent of the total SR registrants that live on the fractional block. BLKREG is the number of registered voters on the fractional block.
On this page: how you estimated the 2024 votes in each of the new districts: the approach you chose and the assumption it rests on, the estimated votes for each party in each new district, and a check of whether your allocation kept every vote.


Part 6: Results
This is the first page of your dashboard, so take care to present your results in a manner that is clear and makes the most important comparison easy: the 2024 congressional results against a hypothetical re-run of the 2024 election using the new district map. If there is another visualization or statistic that you find insightful and effective, you’re welcome to add it.
To draw the maps, download the 2024 district shapefiles, and the AB 604 shapefiles if you don’t have them yet from Part 5. As in Part 5, unzip them into data/shapefiles/ so that git ignores them:

2024 Congressional Districts: shapefiles for the congressional districts in effect for the 2024 election (choose California).
Proposed Congressional Map: shapefiles for the district map in AB 604.

On this page: the headline comparison between the 2024 results and your re-run of the 2024 election on the AB 604 map. Show maps of both sets of districts, each district colored by the party that won it (for the AB 604 map, in your re-run), and for both maps, the number of seats won by Democrats, the mean-median score, and the efficiency gap. Close with your answer to the research question and its caveats.

igraph (network analysis & static plots)

accepts adjacency matrices.

networkD3 (interactive plots)

expects data frames of nodes and edges, not a network object.
nodes are the names/points in the resulting plot

title: Lab 2
text:

Random sociomatrix = ties assigned by chance
Observed monk network = structured by social dynamics
Key question: What features do we see in the real network that random ones lack?

Shows the complexity of real social systems

title: Spatial Data II
text:
Last Time

A coordinate system locates points from an origin.
A datum models the shape of the earth.
A projection flattens the globe and distorts it.
A simple feature pairs a geometry with attributes.


Key Ideas for Today

An sf object is a data frame plus geometries.
Unary functions measure or reshape a geometry.
Binary predicates test how two geometries relate.
A spatial join matches rows by location.



Concept Acquisition

Spatial data come from R packages and web APIs, shapefiles, GeoJSON, and KML.
An sf object is a data frame of attributes plus a geometry column (an sfc) built from individual st_ geometries and a CRS.
dplyr verbs work on the attributes of an sf object and carry the geometry along; summarize() also combines the geometries.
Unary measures (dimension, area, length) return a number for each geometry; unary transformers (centroid, jitter, buffer) return a new geometry.
A binary predicate such as within tests how two geometries relate; a spatial join uses one to match rows, keeping (left) or dropping (inner) unmatched rows.

Tool Acquisition

st_read(), st_geometry(), and base plot() / points().
st_point(), st_polygon(), st_sfc(), and st_sf().
st_dimension(), st_area(), st_length(), st_centroid(), st_jitter(), and st_buffer().
st_within() and st_join() with join = and left =.

Concept Application

Predict the rows and columns of a left join with st_within (timed, 1:00).
PS 5: map the centroid of California (and, as a challenge, find its county with a spatial join); build lines and a polygon from scratch, compute their measures, split the polygon with the lines, and join the pieces to a triangle.

title: Spatial Data II
text:
(Last Time) Simple Feature Object:
Features: “things” or objects that have a spatial location or extent; they may be physical objects like a building, or social conventions like a political state
Feature geometry: the spatial properties (location or extent) of a feature, and can be described by a point, a point set, a polygon, etc.
Feature attributes: other non-spatial properties measured on the feature (e.g. color, name, landtype)

title: Spatial Data II
text:
Guess the Metaphor



A spatial join is like the pirate islands: the islands are polygons and the ships are points. To learn whose waters each ship sails in, you match them by location, not by a shared key, and a ship out in open water finds no island at all.

title: Dates and Times II
text:
Last Time

A date-time counts seconds since 1970 (Unix time).
Parsing turns text into a date-time.
Getters and setters read and change its parts.
Some parts, like months, are circular.


Key Ideas for Today

A duration is a fixed span in seconds.
A period is a span in human units.
UTC is the world’s reference clock.
A time zone is an offset from UTC.



Concept Acquisition

Subtracting two dates gives a difftime, whose units vary.
A duration measures a span in exact seconds, so adding one ignores daylight saving time and leap years.
A period measures a span in human units (days, weeks, years) whose length in seconds varies.
UTC is the global time standard; each time zone is an offset from it, identified in R by an Olson name.
Changing a time zone can either keep the instant and change how it prints, or keep the clock reading and change the instant.

Tool Acquisition

today(), ymd(), and ymd_hms(tz =).
as.duration() and the duration constructors dseconds() through dyears().
as.period() and the period constructors seconds() through years().
interval().
Sys.timezone(), OlsonNames(), with_tz(), and force_tz().

Concept Application

Compute an age as a duration and as a period, and the age one year from now.
Predict the result of adding one day to 1 am on the day daylight saving time starts, as a duration and as a period.
Sketch the tidy and the raw data frames behind “The City that Sleeps,” which compares transit in two time zones.

title: Dates and Times II
text:
Duration


In lubridate, a time span with a fixed length in seconds. It tracks physical time, so it ignores irregularities in the calendar like daylight saving time and leap years.


Make one by coercing a difftime with as.duration() or with a constructor function:



dseconds(15)

dminutes(10)

dhours(c(12, 24))

[1] "43200s (~12 hours)" "86400s (~1 days)"

[4] "259200s (~3 days)"

dyears(1)

[1] "31557600s (~1 years)"

title: Dates and Times II
text:
Please answer the following two questions. I will call on someone randomly after the timer is up.

How long is a day?
How long is a year?


  
    −
    +

This is a revisit of the opening question.
Point out that actually “days” don’t have a single fixed length. Most days are 24 hours but at the edge of daylight savings time, its shorter or longer. Same with leap years. So if you talk about the average day or year length, it’s not quite 24 hrs or 365 days.

title: Dates and Times II
text:
Period


In lubridate, a time span that is like a duration except it doesn’t have a fixed length in seconds. It tracks human units (day, week) that are responsive to irregularities.


Example period constructors:

minutes(10)

[1] "21d 0H 0M 0S"

years(1)

Interval


In lubridate, a time span with a specific start and end. Because it knows where it starts, it can be measured in seconds or in calendar units.





leap <- interval(ymd("2024-01-01"),
                 ymd("2025-01-01"))
leap

[1] 2024-01-01 UTC--2025-01-01 UTC

as.duration(leap)

[1] "31622400s (~1 years)"

as.period(leap)

[1] "1y 0m 0d 0H 0M 0S"



How old will I be in a year?

my_age_i <- interval(b, a)
as.period(my_age_i)

[1] "43y 7m 26d 0H 0M 0S"

as.period(my_age_i) + years(1)

[1] "44y 7m 26d 0H 0M 0S"

title: Dates and Times II
text:
Guess the Metaphor



Time zones are like the chrono chaos ruins: one clock tower stands upright while the world around it splinters into shards that don’t line up. UTC is the tower; every time zone is a shard set at its own angle, and daylight saving time knocks some of them askew twice a year.

title: Strings II
text:
Last Time

A string is a sequence of characters in quotes.
A backslash escapes a character’s usual meaning.
A regular expression describes a text pattern.
Metacharacters let one pattern match many strings.


Key Ideas for Today

Shortcut classes name common sets like digits.
Anchors pin a pattern to the start or end.
Grouping sets the scope of a quantifier.
Alternation matches one pattern or another.



On the pinned board, continue the regex toolkit from Strings I. Add each new tool as it appears: ranges and negation, shortcut classes, anchors, grouping, alternation.
Concept Acquisition

A character class matches any one character from a set; ^ at its start negates it and - expresses a range.
Shortcut classes (\d, \s, \w and their capitals) name common sets, and need a second backslash inside an R string.
Anchors (^, $) match positions, not characters, so they pin a pattern to the start or end of a string.
Parentheses group characters so a quantifier applies to the whole group, and | matches one pattern or another; grouping limits how far an alternation reaches.

Tool Acquisition

Regex syntax: ^, $, [...], [^...], [a-z], \\d, \\s, \\w, (), and |.
str_view(..., match = NA), str_count(), and str_extract() from stringr.
A regex tester such as https://regexr.com/.

Concept Application

Write patterns for file names: a webp extension, images starting with p, and a three-digit number.
Write patterns for license plates, spellings of “color”, and valid phone numbers.
Predict which strings "^cat|dog$" and "^(cat|dog)$" match.
Extract the file name from each path with str_extract().

title: Strings II
text:
Ranges and Negation

Special characters in a set:

^ at the start negates the set.
- expresses a range.




x <- "abcd ABCD 12345 -!@#%."







str_view(x, "[a-z]+")



[1] │ <abcd> ABCD 12345 -!@#%.





str_view(x, "[^a-z0-9]+")



[1] │ abcd< ABCD >12345< -!@#%.>



On the pinned board: “^ inside [ ] = not; ^ outside = start.” Return to it at Anchors.
Ask: is there a shorter way to write the warm-up’s [0123456789]{3}? Hold the answer for the recap at the end of this section.

title: Joins and Pivots
text:
Last Time

EDA uncovers structure and generates new questions.
Explanatory plots tell one story to one audience.
Labels and scales clarify and focus comparisons.
Themes and set aesthetics polish the look.


Key Ideas for Today

A join matches the rows of two data frames on a key.
Mutating joins add columns from a second table.
Filtering joins keep or drop rows, adding no columns.
Pivots reshape data longer or wider, toward tidy data.



Concept Acquisition

A join links the rows of two data frames through a key column; the key can have different names in each (join_by(name == Name)).
The four mutating joins (left, right, full, inner) add the columns of y to x and differ only in which unmatched rows they keep.
The two filtering joins (semi, anti) keep or drop rows of x based on whether they match y, and add no columns.
When a key value appears more than once in y, a left join returns every combination of matches, so it can add rows.
Tidy data puts each variable in a column, each observation in a row, and each value in a cell; the same data can be stored in tidy and untidy shapes.

Tool Acquisition

left_join(), right_join(), full_join(), inner_join(), semi_join(), and anti_join(), with by = join_by().
pivot_longer(data, cols, names_to, values_to) and pivot_wider(data, names_from, values_from) from tidyr.
unite() to combine columns into one.

Concept Application

Sketch the data frame that combines sw1 and sw2, then predict the dimensions of each join before running it.
Predict the dimensions of left_join(sw1, sw3) versus left_join(sw3, sw1).
Replace filter() with a semi join and mutate() + case_when() with a left join on the penguins data.
Move between table1, table2, table3, and table4a with pivots and unite().

text:
Joins
A join is an operation that combines two data frames by linking the rows by their unique identifier called a key.
This can be done in six ways.



Left join
Right join
Full join
Inner join
Semi join
Anti join





Annotate joins 1-4 with “Mutating” and joins 5-6 with “Filtering”

title: Joins and Pivots
text:
Guess the Metaphor



A join is like a bridge town: two settlements (data frames) linked at a single crossing (the key). Who gets across, and what they bring with them, depends on the kind of join.

title: Joins and Pivots
text:
Key Ideas for Today

A join matches the rows of two data frames on a key.
Mutating joins add columns from a second table.
Filtering joins keep or drop rows, adding no columns.
Pivots reshape data longer or wider, toward tidy data.

title: Reading and Writing Data
text:
Last Time

Data cleaning is a set of decisions to ensure the data meets expections given its context and intended use.
Clean reproducibly: raw data is read-only; changes lives in code.
Audit a data set against a checklist before analyzing.


Key Ideas for Today

Plain text files store characters; binary files need special software.
YAML, CSV, and JSON add structure to plain text.



Concept Acquisition

Plain text files store characters, binary files (PDF, Excel) need specific software to decode.
Plain text formats span a spectrum of structure, from none (.txt) to tabular (.csv) to nested (.yml, .json), and the structure determines the R object you get back (character vector, data frame, list).

Tool Acquisition

readLines() / writeLines() and read_lines() / write_lines() for .txt.
read.csv() / write.csv() and read_csv() / write_csv() for .csv.
read_yaml() / write_yaml(), fromJSON() / toJSON() / write_json(), and excel_sheets() / read_excel().

Concept Application

Explain why read.csv() reads "13,047" as character while read_csv() parses it as a number.
Request personal data exports for Project 3, looking for multiple files and at least one JSON.

title: Reading and Writing Data
text:
Plain Text File


A file that stores only characters, so it can be opened and read by any text editor, by cat in the shell, or by readLines() in R.





Binary File


A file that stores raw bytes meant to be decoded by specific software. Opened as text, it looks like gibberish.





Every file is bytes on a disk. Only plaintext encodes characters you can read.

title: Reading and Writing Data
text:
Binary Files: PDF and Excel


PDF (.pdf)

Describes a printed page: fonts, positions, images
Great for humans to read
Data inside a PDF table is hard to get back out


Excel (.xlsx)

A zipped bundle of files: cell values, formulas, formatting, multiple sheets
Requires Excel or a package like readxl to decode

Reading and writing data is like working the docks: cargo (data) arrives packed in containers (files). Some crates you can pry open by hand (plain text); others need special tools (binary). Reading unloads the cargo into town (R); writing packs it back up to ship out.

title: The Grammar of Graphics
text:
Last Time

A Quarto document mixes prose and code in a single .qmd file.
Format text using Markdown syntax.
Embed code cells with options to control evaluation and display.
Configure the metadata (YAML) to set its format and options.


Key Ideas for Today

A visual channel visually encodes variation in data.
An aesthetic mapping links a variable to a visual channel.
A geometry determines how obs are drawn on the plot.
Mapping an aesthetic to a variable is different from setting it to a constant.



Concept Acquisition

Plots that look different (histogram, density, box plot, bar chart, scatterplot) share a common underlying structure.
A plot can be decomposed into data, aesthetic mappings, and a geometry.
Visual channels differ in how well they encode ordered versus unordered variables.
Mapping an aesthetic to a variable encodes variation in the data; setting it to a constant does not.

Tool Acquisition

ggplot() to create the canvas and aes() to declare mappings.
Common aesthetics: x, y, color, fill, size, shape, alpha.
Common geometries: geom_point(), geom_bar()/geom_col(), geom_line(), geom_histogram(), geom_boxplot(), geom_violin(), geom_density().
Adding layers with + (not |>).

Concept Application

Identify what the a series of plots have in common and how they differ.
Name the aesthetic mappings and geometries in a multi-variable scatterplot.
Translate a plot into ggplot2 code, and vice versa.

title: The Grammar of Graphics
text:
Mapping an aesthetic
Mapping connects an aesthetic to a variable in the data frame, so it varies from mark to mark. Mappings go inside aes().

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm,
             y = flipper_length_mm,
             color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_gray(base_size = 18)

title: The Grammar of Graphics
text:
Setting an aesthetic
Setting fixes an aesthetic to a constant value, so every mark looks the same. Settings go outside aes(), as an argument to the geom_().

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm,
             y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  theme_gray(base_size = 18)

git tracks changes to files.

Concept Acquisition

git is a free, open-source command-line tool for tracking changes to files, built to coordinate collaborative coding; it lets you save work, document your process, share, and collaborate.
A repository is a directory tracked by git; changes move from working directory to staging area (add) to a saved snapshot (commit).
A commit pairs a snapshot with a message, building a history you can review with git log.
GitHub hosts remote repos so work can be shared and synced across machines and collaborators.

git remote add, git push -u origin main, git clone.

Edit a file, then stage and commit the change to build a two-commit history.
Create a GitHub repo, link it as origin, and push local commits to it.

text:
Last Time

A function bundles code into a reusable tool.
Functions created with function(), saved as objects.
Arguments make it flexible; defaults make it quick.

Key Ideas for Today

A factor stores categorical data as integer with levels lookup.
An object’s class lets functions behave differently.
Ordered factors allow meaningful sorting.
A data frame is a named list of equal-length vectors.
Data frames subset like a list $, [[]], [] and like a matrix [r,c].



Concept Acquisition

A factor encodes categorical data as an integer vector paired with a levels attribute, which is more compact than a character vector and preserves meaning.
An object’s class attribute lets generic functions like summary() dispatch different behavior — a first taste of object-oriented programming.
Ordered factors (ordered = TRUE) can be sorted meaningfully, not just alphabetically.
Atomic vectors, matrices, and lists are each insufficient for storing related, mixed-type, rectangular data.
A data frame is a named list of equal-length vectors, giving it both list-like and matrix-like subsetting.

Tool Acquisition

data.frame(), names(), row.names(), str(), dim(), nrow(), ncol().

Add a level and reorder a factor sensibly, then re-plot.
Construct a data frame using dataframe().
Subset a data frame using both matrix- and list-style syntax.

title: Control Flow
text:
Last Time

A list is a non-atomic vector: types can be mixed.
[] subsets a list and returns a list.
[[ ]] and $ return the object inside the list.
Lists can nest, so subsetting can be chained.
$ allows subsetting by name.


Key Ideas for Today

Use comparison operators to compare two values.
if-then runs code only when a condition is TRUE.
if-else chooses between two blocks of code based on condition.
A for loop repeats code for each element of a vector.
ifelse() is a vectorized if-else.



Concept Acquisition

If-then executes code only when its condition evaluates to TRUE; otherwise nothing happens.
If-else guarantees that exactly one of two blocks runs.
Chaining else if clauses lets a decision tree with many branches be expressed in R.
A for loop repeats an action once per element, with a loop variable taking each value (or index) in turn.
Wrapping an if-then inside a for loop applies conditional logic element-by-element; ifelse() does the same thing vectorized, without an explicit loop.

Tool Acquisition

if (condition) { ... }
if (condition) { ... } else { ... }
if (condition) { ... } else if (condition) { ... } else { ... }
for (item in vector) { ... }
ifelse(test, yes, no)

Concept Application

Translate a decision tree (e.g. how to get to campus) into nested if-then statements.
Predict the output of a for loop paired with an if statement, run over a vector of random values.
Rewrite an explicit for + if loop as a single vectorized ifelse() call.

title: Extending Vectors

An atomic vector holds elements of a single type.

Key Ideas for Today

Comments mark text that R will not evaluate.

Concept Acquisition

The comment character # stops evaluation for the rest of the line.
Assigning into a subset changes a vector in place; names can be changed the same way.

Matrices are subset by index, by name, or by logical, along rows and columns; an empty index means “all”.
Some data are naturally indexed by two sets of labels (e.g. who rated whom).

title: Intro to R
text:
Last Time

Data is stored on a computer disk in files.
Files are stored in directories.
Files and directories can be structured using a tree.
Each file’s location is defined by its path.
A UNIX shell is used to modify the file system.


Key Ideas for Today

R evaluates expressions like a calculator.
Functions take arguments and can have defaults.
Values can be saved as objects in the environment.
An R session, like the shell, has a working directory.
Warnings vs. errors.



Concept Acquisition

R evaluates expressions, like a calculator.
Functions take arguments (by position or by name) and can have defaults.
Values can be saved as objects in the environment.
An R session, like the shell, has a working directory.
Warnings vs. errors.

Tool Acquisition

Arithmetic and sqrt(), log().
<- for assignment; ? for help.
getwd(), list.files(), setwd(), readLines().
as.numeric(), mean(), sd(), summary().

Concept Application

Predict the output of a chain of assignments and arithmetic.
Call a function using arguments by position and by name.
Navigate the file system from within R and read a file’s contents.
Convert character data to numeric and summarize it.

This lecture is live-coded. Bring up the R console with the drop plugin (press `) and use the chalkboard to annotate.

Shell Command Options
In addition to path arguments, shell commands have options that change the way they work.

A few ls options:



Option
Meaning




-l

-h

-R

title: Intro to R
text:
Structure of an R function


Function


A named procedure that takes arguments (inputs) and returns a value. Arguments can be supplied by position or by name, and some have default values.



Live-code the one at a time. Draw out the anatomy on the chalkboard: function name, then arguments inside ().

log(10) uses the default base e.
Naming an argument (base = 10) is unambiguous.
By position, the second argument is base, so log(10, 5) and log(5, 10) differ.
When you name every argument, order stops mattering: log(base = 5, x = 10).
You can learn more about the function by pulling up it’s help file with ?

log(10)
log(10, base = 10)
?log
log(10, base = 5)
log(10, 5)
log(5, 10)
log(base = 5, x = 10)

title: Intro to R
text:
Creating objects


Object


A value saved into your environment under a name, using the assignment arrow <-. Calling the name on its own prints the value.

title: Intro to R
text:
Creating objects
a <- 3 + 5      # save the result into an object named a
print(a)
a               # calling an object invokes print()
a + 2
a <- a + 2      # overwrite a with a new value
ls()            # list objects in environment

Emphasize that <- does not print anything — the value is stored. Show the object appearing in the Environment. The last line is worth pausing on: the right side is computed first, then assigned back to a.

title: Intro to R
text:
The R environment


Environment


The collection of all objects currently defined in your R session, each stored under its name. Assignment adds or updates an object in the environment; ls() lists what it contains.



Tie this back to the previous slide: the objects created with <- all live in the environment. Show the Environment pane so students can see the names and values accumulating as they run code.

title: Intro to R
text:
From the shell to R
Last time we moved around the file system at the command line. An R session has the same idea of a working directory — and its own functions to get around.




Task
Shell
R




Where am I?
pwd
getwd()


What’s around me?
ls
list.files()


Change where I am
cd
setwd()


See a file’s contents
cat
readLines()




On the board, sketch the file system tree and draw two boxes next to it, one labelled “shell” and one labelled “R”. Both have a working directory that you can move. Then live-code the R column.

title: Intro to R
section: Where am I? What’s around me?
text:
Where am I? What’s around me?
getwd()
ls()            # careful: lists objects, not files!
list.files()
setwd()
system("tree .")

The gotcha: ls() in R lists objects in your environment, not files on disk — a false friend from the shell. list.files() is the file lister. system("tree .") shells out to draw the tree we studied last time.

title: Intro to R
text:
Moving and reading files
setwd("data-in-trees/blue/stat/101/1")
cat("109.txt")          # not what you'd expect...
readLines("109.txt")

cat("108.txt") prints the string 108.txt, not the file — a nice teachable surprise. Ask Gemini for the function that reads a file; land on readLines(). Reading 108.txt produces a warning about an incomplete final line — segue to the next slide.

title: Intro to R
text:
Warnings and errors


Warning


A message telling you something might be off. The code still runs and returns a value.





Error


A message telling you the code could not run. No value is returned.

title: Intro to R
text:
Warnings and errors
setwd("../../../non-stat")
readLines("100/1/100.txt")   # note the typo

Move the working directory up and over with a relative path (reinforcing last lecture). Then deliberately fumble the path — — to trigger a “cannot open file” error. Contrast: the warning earlier still returned the file’s lines; this error returns nothing.

title: Intro to R
section: How far did we travel this summer?
text:
How far did we travel this summer?
Recall the second question on your index card: the farthest you were from Cal this summer, in miles.

All of those values have been pulled out of the individual files and stacked into one:
find . -type f -name "*.txt" -print0 \
  | xargs -0 awk 'FNR==2 && /^[0-9,]+$/' \
  > combined_output.txt

This connects today’s tools back to the index-card data from lectures 1–2. Don’t dwell on the find | xargs | awk incantation — just note that the command line let us grab the second line of every file and combine them. This is why the command line is worth knowing.

title: Intro to R
text:
Reading the distances into R
readLines("combined_output.txt")
distances <- readLines("combined_output.txt")

mean(distances)      # whoops — a mean of character strings

readLines() gives us a value per line, but each is a character string. mean() on characters returns NA with a warning. Ask the students what went wrong before revealing the fix.

title: Intro to R
text:
Converting and summarizing
distances <- as.numeric(distances)   # text -> numbers
mean(distances)
sd(distances)
summary(distances)

as.numeric() coerces the strings to numbers; now the summaries work. Read summary() together — min, quartiles, median, mean, max — as a first look at the distribution. If any value fails to convert it becomes NA; watch for that.

A named container that stores data – such as text, images, or programs – on a computer disk. The file name usually ends in an extension (.txt, .png, .pdf) that indicates the format.

text:
How can we specify the location of a file/directory in the file system?



Path


A description of a file or directory’s location in the file system, written as a sequence of folder names that leads to it, separated by /.

Absolute path: Starts from the root of the file system, indicated by /. Example: /Documents/Schoolwork/HW1.pdf

title: Data in Trees
text:
How can we specify the location of a file/directory in the file system?


Path


A description of a file or directory’s location in the file system, written as a sequence of folder names that leads to it, separated by /.
Absolute path: Starts from the root of the file system, indicated by /. Example: /Documents/Schoolwork/HW1.pdf
Relative path: Starts from the current directory and shows how to reach a target. .. means “go up one level”. Example if you’re in Documents, Schoolwork/HW1.pdf



Ask: What relative paths are found in our tree?
On the board pick at least two relative paths for them to give you, one that goes from a directory to a file in a subdirectory, and another that requires going “up one level” to a file in a differet directory at the same level. You can indiated the “start” and “end” of the relative path using, say a square and a triangle.

title: Data in Trees
text:
I’m getting tired of always typing the trunk of the tree…



Home directory


A special designated directory in a file system that serves as a starting point for commonly-used paths.
Written as ~, a shorthand for its absolute path.

ls


Lists the contents of your present working directory.



UNIX is a family of operating systems that includes Linux and MacOS. Most of the commands work on windows too.

cd


Changes your directory to the path provided (after a space). Examples:

cd Homework: (relative) only takes you into the Homework directory if you’re in Documents.
cd /Document/Homework: (absolute) takes you into the Homework directory regardless of your pwd.






cat


Prints to the screen the contents of the file at the path provided. Example: cat 127.txt.

What are the names of the files stored in ~/data-in-trees/red/stat/101/1/?1

One way is to move into the directory, then list its contents:
cd ~/data-in-trees/red/stat/101/1/
ls
012.txt  014.txt


Or list the contents without moving, by giving ls the path directly:
ls ~/data-in-trees/red/stat/101/1/
012.txt  014.txt

The trailing / isn’t strictly necessary here, but it’s good practice as it signals that the path points to a directory rather than a file.

title: Data in Trees
text:
Solution 2
What is the absolute path of the file named 014.txt?

An absolute path starts from the root /. Searching the tree, 014.txt lives inside red/stat/101/1/, so relative to home it is:
~/data-in-trees/red/stat/101/1/014.txt


Remember ~ is shorthand for home’s absolute path. On DataHub home is /home/jovyan, so the fully-written absolute path is:
/home/jovyan/data-in-trees/red/stat/101/1/014.txt


You can confirm the home path by running pwd after cd ~.

title: Data in Trees
text:
Solution 3
What is the relative path of the file named 014.txt from ~/data-in-trees/red/non-stat?

From red/non-stat, step up one level (..) to red, then descend into stat/101/1/:
../stat/101/1/014.txt


Check it from that starting directory by printing the file at the relative path:
cat ../stat/101/1/014.txt
lebi tirar mas fotos
5200

title: Data in Trees
text:
Solution 4
What is the relative path of the directory at ~/data-in-trees/green/stat/ from ~/data-in-trees/red/non-stat?

From red/non-stat, step up two levels: .. reaches red, and ../.. reaches data-in-trees. Then descend into green/stat:
../../green/stat


The two colors (red, green) sit at the same level, so any path between them must first climb up to their shared parent, data-in-trees.


Check it by walking the path yourself. First confirm where you are:
pwd
/home/jovyan/data-in-trees/red/non-stat


Then follow the relative path and confirm you arrived:
cd ../../green/stat
pwd
/home/jovyan/data-in-trees/green/stat

title: Data in Trees
text:
Solution 5
What is the song of the summer in ~/data-in-trees/red/non-stat/101/1/003.txt?

Print the file’s contents with cat:
cat ~/data-in-trees/red/non-stat/101/1/003.txt


which shows:
lebi tirar mas fotos
5200


So the song is lebi tirar mas fotos (the second line, 5200, is the accompanying count).


Alternatively, cd into the file’s directory first, then cat just the bare file name:
cd ~/data-in-trees/red/non-stat/101/1/
cat 003.txt
lebi tirar mas fotos
5200

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Last Time

R evaluates expressions like a calculator.
Functions take arguments and can have defaults.
Values can be saved as objects in the environment.
An R session, like the shell, has a working directory.
Warnings vs. errors.


Key Ideas for Today

An atomic vector holds elements of a single type.
Special values mark data that is missing or undefined.
Operations are vectorized and vectors are recycled.
Mixing types triggers coercion.
Elements are pulled out by subsetting.



Concept Acquisition

An atomic vector is an ordered collection of elements of the same type.
The four common types: logical, integer, double, character.
NULL, NA, NaN, and Inf behave differently from one another.
Vectorization and vector recycling.
Implicit coercion follows a hierarchy; explicit coercion is done by hand.
Subsetting by index, by name, and by logical.

Tool Acquisition

c(), typeof(), length().
:, seq(), rep().
na.rm = TRUE.
as.double() and friends.
vec[...].

Concept Application

Predict the type of a vector built from mixed inputs.
Write the shortest command that generates a given vector.
Predict the result of arithmetic on vectors of unequal length.
Extract a subset of elements three different ways.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Atomic Vectors


Atomic Vector


R’s principal data structure: an ordered collection of elements of the same type. Created with the c() function (for combine).



Draw a row of boxes on the board — an ordered sequence of cells, each holding one element. Emphasize ordered (position matters) and same type (no mixing).

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
The four common types
dbl_vec  <- c(3, 5, 1.2)
int_vec  <- c(3L, 5L, 1L)
char_vec <- c("cat", "dog", "dingo")
log_vec  <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)




Type
Looks like
Note




double
3, 1.2
R’s default for numbers


integer
3L
the L suffix is required


character
"dog"
quotes required


logical
TRUE, FALSE
also T / F, but spell them out




Live-code each assignment, then call the object on its own to print it. Point out the [1] index marker at the start of the printed line. Ask why c(3, 5, 1.2) is a double and not an integer — because 3 without the L is a double.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Inspecting vectors
typeof() returns the type of the vector.
length() returns the number of elements.

typeof(char_vec)
typeof(log_vec)
typeof(dbl_vec)
typeof(int_vec)

length(char_vec)
length(dbl_vec)

These two functions answer the two questions you can ask of any atomic vector: what’s in it? and how many? Run typeof() on all four and read the answers out loud — note "double" not "numeric".

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Guess the metaphor


An atomic vector is like a vineyard, an ordered, 1D set of things of the same type (grapes).

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Three shortcuts
: creates a sequence from the left number to the right, stepping by 1.
seq() creates a sequence from a number to a number by an interval.
rep() replicates a vector times times.

4:8
seq(from = 1, to = 3, by = .1)
seq(1, 3, .1)
rep(1:3, times = 2)

Connect back to the last lecture: seq(1, 3, .1) and seq(from = 1, to = 3, by = .1) are the same call, one by position and one by name. Pull up ?seq and ?rep to show there are more arguments than we’re using (length.out, each) — a hook for the problem set.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Your turn
What three commands will generate the following vectors?
[1] 5.0 5.5 6.0 6.5 7.0
[1]  2  1  0 -1 -2
[1] "cat"   "dog"   "dingo" "cat"   "dog"   "dingo"

  
    −
    +
 
 01:00
 

The middle one is the interesting case: by must be negative to count down. seq(from = 2, to = -2, by = 1) errors — a good moment to read the error message together.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Solutions
seq(from = 5, to = 7, by = .5)
seq(from = 2, to = -2, by = -1)
2:-2        # also works!
rep(char_vec, times = 2)

Note that the third answer reuses an object we already made rather than retyping the strings — that’s the point of saving objects.

title: Atomic Vectors
section: Four values that aren’t ordinary data
text:
Four values that aren’t ordinary data



Value
Meaning




NULL
does not exist


NA
not available / missing


NaN
not a number (e.g. 0/0)


Inf
infinity (e.g. 1/0)




NA is the one you’ll meet constantly in real data. NULL is the odd one: it is the absence of a value, so it takes up no room in a vector. Demonstrate on the board by drawing the row of boxes for c(NA, NULL, 1) — two boxes, not three.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Missing values are contagious
c(NA, NULL, 1)
mean(c(NA, NULL, 1))
mean(c(NA, NULL, 1), na.rm = TRUE)

Ask what length(c(NA, NULL, 1)) will be before running it. Then: why is the mean NA? Because the mean of a set that includes an unknown value is itself unknown — R is being careful, not broken. na.rm = TRUE tells R to drop the missing values first. Stress that this is a choice you are making about your data, not a bug fix.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Your Turn
What will these return?
c(1, 2, 3) + c(2, 3, 4)
c(1, 2, 3) + c(2, 3)
c(1, "dog", TRUE)

  
    −
    +
 
 01:00
 

Poll the room on each line before running it. All three surprise people in different ways, and each one motivates a concept on the next slides: vectorization, recycling, and coercion.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Vectorization and recycling


Vectorization


Operations and functions that run on an entire vector at once, element by element.





Vector Recycling


If an operation needs a longer vector than provided, R reuses the existing elements, in order, from the beginning.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Vectorization and recycling
log(c(2, 6, 1))
c(1, 2, 3) + c(2, 3, 4)
c(1, 2, 3) + c(2, 3)

On the board, write the two vectors next to one another and draw the element-wise pairing. For the recycled case, write the shorter vector out again underneath — 2, 3, 2 — so students see where the third element came from. Note that R warns here because 3 isn’t a multiple of 2; when it is a multiple you get no warning at all, which is what makes recycling dangerous.
In most other languages, adding two collections requires writing a loop. Vectorization is a defining feature of R.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Type coercion


Implicit Coercion


When you mix types, R converts them all to a single type so the vector stays atomic. It follows a hierarchy, always moving up:



Annotate slide with:
logical < integer < double < character
Write the hierarchy on the board as an arrow. The rule: R picks the least-general type that can hold everything. c(1, "dog", TRUE) must go all the way up to character because only character can represent all three.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Implicit coercion
c(1, "dog", TRUE)
c(TRUE, FALSE, 3)
mean(c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE))

The last line is worth dwelling on: TRUE becomes 1 and FALSE becomes 0, so the mean of a logical vector is the proportion of TRUEs. That’s a trick we’ll use over and over once we start filtering data.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Explicit coercion
as.___(x) converts x to the type ___.

distances <- c("2800", "450", "10")
distances
mean(distances)

distances <- as.double(distances)
distances
mean(distances)

This isthe bug from last lecture. readLines() gives us character data; mean() on characters returns NA with a warning. Point out the quotes disappearing in the printed output after coercion.
Ask what as.double("dog") returns. NA, with a warning. Coercion that can’t succeed produces missing values, so always check afterward.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Subsetting by index
vec[index]

char_vec
char_vec[2]
char_vec[2:3]
char_vec[rep(3, 10)]

Annotate the anatomy on the board: the vector, the square bracket, and inside it another numeric vector of positions. That last point is the key insight — the thing inside the brackets is itself a vector, which is why 2:3 and rep(3, 10) both work.
R indexes from 1, unlike Python and most other languages.
The rep(3, 10) example shows the result can be longer than the original.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Subsetting by name
named_char_vec <- c("thrash" = "cat",
                    "buzz" = "dog",
                    "poppy" = "dingo")
named_char_vec
named_char_vec["buzz"]
named_char_vec[rep("poppy", 10)]

Names are an attribute attached to a vector; note how printing changes to show a header row of names. The same pattern holds: whatever is inside the brackets is a vector, here a character vector.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Subsetting by logicals
named_char_vec[c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)]

The logical vector acts as a mask, one entry per element: keep, drop, keep. This is the least intuitive of the three but by far the most useful — next lecture we’ll generate those logicals from comparisons instead of typing them out, and that’s how filtering works.
If time permits, ask what happens when the logical vector is shorter than the vector being subset. Recycling, again.

title: Atomic Vectors
text:
Key Ideas for Today

An atomic vector holds elements of a single type.
Special values mark data that is missing or undefined.
Operations are vectorized and vectors are recycled.
Mixing types triggers coercion.
Elements are pulled out by subsetting.
